hints: Notice the pivot at the mast end of the boom - taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown pivot force from the equation.
The uniform $200 \text{ N}$ boom acts at its centre, so its clockwise moment arm is half the boom length while tension $T$ acts at the full length.
Only the vertical part of the rope tension, $T \sin 40^{\circ}$, is perpendicular to the horizontal boom and provides the anticlockwise moment.
walkthrough: Take moments about the pivot so the unknown contact force at the pivot has zero moment and can be ignored.
The boom is uniform, so the $200 \text{ N}$ weight acts at the midpoint. If boom length is $L$, its clockwise moment is $200 \times L/2 = 100L$.
The rope pulls at $40^{\circ}$ to the horizontal at distance $L$ from the pivot. The perpendicular component is $T \sin 40^{\circ}$ upward.
Its anticlockwise moment about the pivot is $T \sin 40^{\circ} \times L$.
For equilibrium, sum of moments is zero: $T \sin 40^{\circ} \times L = 100L$.
Cancel $L$ and solve: $T = 100/\sin 40^{\circ} \approx 100/0.643 \approx 156 \text{ N}$, about $160 \text{ N}$. This is option B.

options.A: About $130 \text{ N}$ comes from using the full $200 \text{ N}$ at the centre with an incorrect moment arm or trig factor, not $T \sin 40^{\circ}$ balancing half the weight.
options.B: Taking moments about the pivot gives $T \sin 40^{\circ} = 100 \text{ N}$, so $T \approx 156 \text{ N}$, close to $160 \text{ N}$.
options.C: About $260 \text{ N}$ treats the $200 \text{ N}$ weight as acting at the end of the boom instead of at its centre at half the length.
options.D: About $310 \text{ N}$ uses $T \cos 40^{\circ}$ for the vertical component and puts the weight at the end, giving $T = 200/\cos 40^{\circ}$.
